video_title: Portable Alpha, Trend Following & AI Investing ft. Harry Moore | Systematic Investor | Ep.412
gist: Man Group's Harry Moore and host Niels Kaastrup-Larsen use the July 2026 AI-trade unwind (a hedge fund that reached ~$45bn before losing two-thirds) and the yen intervention to argue that most multi-asset books are a single concentrated bet, then walk through the portable-alpha paper Moore co-wrote: hold beta via futures/swaps, keep ~40% cash (10% margin plus 30% unencumbered) to avoid being forcibly degeared, rebalance slowly with tolerance bands, and pick an alpha that is uncorrelated in the left tail. They close on the mathematics-of-turtle-trading paper (range-based vol, unit sizing, 2N stops as fractional Kelly) and on AI collapsing the implementation half of quant research.

themes.theme: AI-trade concentration and left-tail portfolio resilience

insights.claim: A hedge fund built around Leopold Ashenbrenner's AI thesis gathered roughly $45 billion in assets on a very short track record and then lost about two-thirds of it in a matter of weeks in July 2026.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
insights.so_what: A $45bn single-theme vehicle unwinding in weeks is a live warning that AI-theme crowding, not valuation alone, is the near-term source of forced-selling risk in tech.
insights.quote: here someone with very little experience, very little track record um you know ends up having $45 billion or so uh under management before losing um 2/3 of that it seems in in a matter of weeks

insights.claim: A book can look dollar-neutral or market-neutral and still be a concentrated directional bet if both legs are expressions of the same theme, which is how the AI-trade fund was hedged.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Screen alpha managers on thematic exposure, not just gross/net and beta neutrality; theme concentration is the exposure that actually kills the P&L.
insights.quote: even if on paper you look somewhat like dollar neutral or market neutral, your your your theme is is is has kind of caught you out there

insights.claim: Moore deliberately holds both AI scenarios open: the railroad/dotcom capex-mania analogy that ends in tears, and an upside case in which the trade that broke in July 2026 turns out to be the right trade for the next ten years.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: If the honest prior is genuine two-sided uncertainty, position sizing and convexity matter more than picking the AI bubble's top.
insights.quote: Maybe there is this huge upside scenario where um the trade that we saw go wrong last month is the right trade and it works over over the next 10 years.

insights.claim: A conventional allocator book of equities, bonds, commodities and private assets is effectively one long bet on continued AI capex and growth, and in a 30-40% equity drawdown none of those sleeves protects the portfolio.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Stress the whole book against a 30-40% index decline rather than a 5-10% wobble; the diversification that shows up in normal-times correlations disappears exactly when it is needed.
insights.quote: on paper, you look diversified, right? These assets they seem to have kind of in normal times somewhat low correlations with each other.

insights.claim: Bonds and gold both sold off in correlated fashion earlier in 2026, and with US inflation running above target for years the Fed may lack room to cut aggressively, so bonds could sell off hard in the same shock that hits equities.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: The 60/40 rate-cut cushion is conditional on the Fed having room; an inflation-constrained Fed makes duration a poor equity hedge and raises the value of price-following diversifiers.
insights.quote: inflation's now been running above target for many many years. It's not just like it's it's it's a short period. It's it's many years. do they have the tools to really cut rates

insights.claim: Trend following earns its place in an AI-concentrated book because it holds no long-term view, can flip to short bonds and short equities, go long commodities in an inflation shock, and can even short the AI theme itself by selling semis and tech hardware names.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: The relevant test for a diversifier is the covariance matrix in the shock, not the full-sample correlation, and trend is typically zero-to-negatively correlated there.
insights.quote: as an investor when you look and you say okay my assets are are uncorrelated but are they uncorrelated in that left tail shock like what does your coariance matrix look like in that shock

themes.theme: Yen intervention and unsimulatable tail moves

insights.claim: Japanese (and possibly US) authorities intervened in the yen only days before July 2026 month-end, and the move showed up in managed-futures performance for the month.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
insights.so_what: Short-yen was the crowded trend position, so July manager dispersion is largely explained by yen sizing and speed rather than skill.
insights.quote: the central banks of Japan and possibly I guess the US as well intervening uh in the Japanese yen only a couple of days before month end

insights.claim: The yen intervention move was roughly a 10-standard-deviation event, against the 20-30 standard deviations of the Swiss franc de-peg, and such policy-driven moves cannot be reproduced by simulated market data.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host) and Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Backtests and Monte Carlo engines systematically understate intervention risk, so single-position caps rather than model-implied VaR are the real defence, and rules-based systems that hold through the rumour phase must size for it.
insights.quote: That that that does not appear in if you're if you're building market data that's very hard to to actually simulate something like that. But we we know they exist from from time to time.

themes.theme: July-August tape: model speed, sector legs and market universe

insights.claim: As of 11 August 2026 the BTOP50 was down 67bp in the month and up 7.17% YTD, the SG CTA index down 88bp and up 7.15%, the SG Trend index down 94bp and up 6.89%, while the short-term traders index was up 14bp in August but only 3.32% YTD.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
insights.so_what: Trend is up ~7% YTD with a soft start to August, and the short-term sub-strategy is lagging badly, confirming the slow-over-fast regime.
insights.quote: It's still up 7.17% so far this year. The sock gen CG index is down 88 basis points up 7.15% so far this year.

insights.claim: Traditional benchmarks were far stronger in early August 2026: MSCI World up 2.77% in the month and 12.45% YTD, MSCI World ex-US/Canada up 1.83% and 11.8%, the S&P US aggregate bond index up 64bp in the month but only 31bp YTD, and the S&P 500 total return up 3.12% in the month and 12.83% YTD.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
insights.so_what: Equities are compounding while bonds are flat YTD, so the diversification burden in 2026 books sits entirely on non-bond diversifiers.

insights.claim: July 2026 dispersion among trend managers came from the split between rallying energy markets (profitable) and the stalled AI trade, where long semis and tech hardware against short software hurt, so asset-class risk weights and market exclusions determined the month's outcome.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Attribute July manager returns to energy weight and equity-sector exposure rather than to trend skill when doing manager selection.
insights.quote: choices about how much to have within each asset class, how much risk weight to have in that in the long run, choices of whether to exclude certain markets or whole asset classes would have created a lot a lot of dispersion in in July

insights.claim: Running one standard trend model across four lookbacks shows a 20-day speed down YTD in 2026, a 60-day speed down but less, a 130-day speed slightly up and a 260-day speed up the most.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
insights.so_what: Speed is the single biggest explanator of 2026 trend dispersion; allocators should ask managers for their effective lookback before judging performance.
insights.quote: if you had chosen a 20-day look back, again, this is just from this specific model, um, you would actually have been down uh, this year.

insights.claim: Slow trend models won in 2026 because they stayed persistently short bonds, held long energy positions longer and stayed long equities throughout, and no turning point has persisted long enough for fast models to shine.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: The slow-outperforms regime has run several years now, but Moore still argues for dynamic speed so the book can capture the eventual turning point.
insights.quote: we haven't had a a a turning point that that's that's persisted for long enough for for for the faster speeds to to kind of shine

insights.claim: Alternative markets underperformed traditional ones in 2026: Nordic and Italian power stayed rangebound while mid-frequency models made money in Brent and heating oil, and alternative rates such as Polish interest-rate swaps gyrated more than 10-year Treasuries or gilts.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: The alternative-markets premium that justified higher fees has been a drag this year, so compare managers on market universe before attributing 2026 gaps to skill.
insights.quote: those markets have have just tended to be a little bit more rangebound than we've seen in the more traditional energy markets this year

insights.claim: Cross-sectional equity models on cash sectors and factors (semis versus software, value, momentum, quality) were profitable in 2026 but in a completely different way to index trend, with the quality factor itself struggling year to date.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Cross-sectional equity alpha is a genuinely separate return stream from index trend and should be sized as a diversifier rather than a substitute.
insights.quote: quality has really struggled this year on a year-to- date basis

themes.theme: Portable alpha cash buffers and knockout risk

insights.claim: Because trend runs on futures, an investor needs only about $20-25 of capital to obtain $100 of trend exposure, so adding trend does not require selling down an existing portfolio.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: The 'what do I sell to fund it' objection to trend allocations is largely a misunderstanding of margin requirements; the real constraint is governance, not cash.
insights.quote: if I only need to use $20 or $25 to get my $100 of trend following gives me a few new levers and things that I can do with the freed up cash

insights.claim: The portable alpha structure in Man Group's paper sells no equity at all: passive index exposure is held via a future or swap and a trend allocation is layered on top, aiming to deliver the index plus alpha.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Framing trend as an overlay rather than a substitute removes the benchmark-relative career risk that blocks most trend allocations.
insights.quote: I'm going to sell essentially no equity exposure, right? I'm going to keep my portfolio exactly as it was.

insights.claim: Beta held on derivatives can be supported with as little as $10 of capital per $100 of exposure, freeing $90 for alpha, but that is precisely the configuration that caused portable alpha structures to fail in 2008 through insufficient liquidity and alpha-beta correlation.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Maximum capital efficiency in the structure is exactly what converts a market drawdown into forced deleveraging; the 2008 failure modes have not been engineered away.
insights.quote: we know that in 2008 many of these structures failed right and the lines down which those structures failed those risks still exist

insights.claim: Simulating an S&P-plus-trend portable alpha structure with a 20% cash buffer over the past 26-27 years shows the buffer fully drawn down three times: in the dotcom bust, the GFC and COVID.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: A 20% buffer means being forced out of beta roughly once a decade, which is a design flaw rather than a tail event.
insights.quote: that gets fully drawn down three times

insights.claim: Being knocked out of the beta leg is costly twice over: an allocator goes from 100% to perhaps 20% index exposure creating massive tracking error, and de-gearing at the early-2009 low would have missed roughly 29-30% of the subsequent upside.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Quantifying forced-degearing as ~30% of foregone rebound turns the cash-buffer decision from an operational detail into the dominant driver of long-run outcomes.
insights.quote: if you were were selling in the early part of 2009 at a at a low in your equity component and you're knocked out that position, you miss kind of 29 30% of of upside

insights.claim: The paper concludes that roughly 40% cash supporting the beta leg (10% margin plus 30% unencumbered) reduces forced de-gearing to about a one-in-100 to one-in-200-year event, validated with Monte Carlo rather than the single realised market path.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: This is the concrete design number for anyone building or buying a portable alpha sleeve: 40% cash against beta, not the 10-20% that maximises alpha capacity.
insights.quote: in the paper we end up with essentially 40% cash to support your beta. So that's 10% margin, 30% unencumbered

themes.theme: Portable alpha rebalancing, instruments and alpha selection

insights.claim: Choosing a monthly rebalance between the beta and alpha legs means the structure stops replicating the index, because selling into a rising index breaks compounding and produces year-end tracking error investors do not expect.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Anyone promising index-plus-alpha on a monthly rebalance is quietly delivering something other than the index; ask the provider to show realised tracking error.
insights.quote: If it goes to 110 and you sell $10 of it to rebalance, you're no longer tracking the index.

insights.claim: In 2008 every rebalancing rule other than buy-and-hold underperformed because rebalancing repeatedly bought falling equities with the proceeds of rising trend, yet over the long run the choice of monthly, quarterly, annual or 5-10% tolerance bands makes almost no performance difference.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Rebalancing frequency is a path-risk decision, not a return decision, so pick the rule by which crisis paths you can tolerate, not by backtest average.
insights.quote: essentially all rules other than a buy and hold underperform in 2008

insights.claim: Man Group's practical recommendation is not pure buy-and-hold (which drifts and complicates subscriptions at NAV) but slow rebalancing with a sensible tolerance band, such as rebalancing only when beta and alpha drift more than 10% out of line.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Tolerance-band rebalancing is the implementable middle ground that keeps index tracking tight without creating drift problems for pooled vehicles.
insights.quote: if you can let that that beta replicate closely, so rebalance a little bit less, but have some sensible tolerance

insights.claim: The swap-versus-future choice in portable alpha has no structural performance advantage: a bank's explicit ~40bp swap spread is implicit in the future and washes out over time, leaving operational preference and counterparty risk as the deciding factors.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Do not pay for an instrument-selection 'edge' in portable alpha; negotiate on operations, collateral terms and counterparty exposure instead.
insights.quote: whereas there's an explicit cost in the swap it's implicit in the future And if you run this over time, it washes out, right? The you don't get a a a structural performance advantage.

insights.claim: A good portable alpha engine must be super liquid so the structure can be recapitalised quickly, which is why trend is a natural candidate, and most institutional investors want the manager to absorb the margin and cash-flow complexity rather than field margin calls themselves.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Alpha sleeves with weekly or monthly dealing terms are structurally unsuited to portable alpha regardless of their standalone Sharpe.
insights.quote: They do not want to be getting margin calls um on a Monday. Please send cash by by end of day.

insights.claim: A 50/50 equity-bond portfolio carries roughly 85% of its risk in equities and 15% in bonds, so the risk-balanced optimum is closer to 30% equities and 70% bonds, a portfolio nobody accepts unlevered because its return is too low.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Leverage is what converts a higher-Sharpe risk-balanced allocation into an acceptable return level; refusing leverage means accepting an equity-dominated risk profile.
insights.quote: 85% of the risk is equities, 15% is bonds, even though on paper it says 50/50

insights.claim: The ported alpha must not itself be more beta, because layering an additional directional equity-like driver on top of 100% beta increases volatility and enlarges the left tail rather than diversifying it.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Screen portable alpha engines for hidden equity beta first; equity-like alpha in a levered stack is the fastest route to the structure failing.
insights.quote: You almost certainly don't want to be introducing more beta, right? That's a risk in the same direction.

insights.claim: The correct test for a ported alpha is not full-sample correlation but correlation in the worst 5% of beta returns, because liquidity-provision strategies like short volatility, merger arbitrage and the Treasury basis trade look excellent in normal times and break precisely in the shock.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Run the conditional-correlation screen on the worst 5% of equity months before approving any alpha for a levered stack; it disqualifies most carry-like strategies.
insights.quote: What you also need to really investigate is not just that it's uncorrelated, but that it's uncorrelated in the left tail.

insights.claim: Trend is uniquely suited to a levered structure because volatility spikes at turning points automatically shrink trend positions, so trend demands less margin exactly when liquidity-provision strategies are getting margin calls.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Vol-scaled position sizing gives trend a negative margin beta in crises, which is the mechanical reason portable alpha with trend survives shocks that kill other stacks.
insights.quote: where people are worried about margin calls, you'd be especially worried about this in like a liquidity provision strategy like the basis trade or other other structures like that. Trend is actually reducing positions.

themes.theme: Turtle rules as early decision theory

insights.claim: The turtles' N was a range-based volatility estimator from open, high, low and close with roughly a 14-day exponential decay half-life, later validated by Parkinson as an efficient way to estimate volatility.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Range-based volatility estimators remain a legitimate, low-data-cost alternative to close-to-close vol in systematic risk models.
insights.quote: the turtles have a property n which is essentially the volatility of of of a market and they use a rangebased estimate estimator very simple to update each day. It's essentially like an exponential decay halfife of 14.

insights.claim: The turtles' 'unit' concept made one unit of crude oil equivalent in risk terms to one unit of 10-year Treasuries even if the Treasury position required five times the dollar amount, which is volatility-based position sizing implemented in the 1980s.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Risk-equalised rather than dollar-equalised sizing is the oldest and most durable feature of trend following, and its absence in a manager's process is a red flag.
insights.quote: such that one unit of each commodity or financial asset they were trading would be equivalent in risk terms

insights.claim: The turtles' 2N stop equated to risking no more than 2% of total equity per position, which the paper links to the Kelly criterion, and their sizing sat well to the left of the Kelly peak, sacrificing upside for a much lower probability of ruin.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Fractional Kelly is the practical standard: any manager sitting at or beyond full Kelly is optimising growth at the cost of survival probability.
insights.quote: any prudent manager will be on the left side of that hill

insights.claim: Unable to invert covariance matrices with pen and paper, the turtles handled correlation between markets through position-size caps on correlated markets rather than inside the portfolio construction.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Caps on correlated clusters are a robust, estimation-error-free substitute for covariance optimisation, useful when correlations are unstable.
insights.quote: they weren't inverting covariance matrices um they had to have rules of thumb

insights.claim: The turtles ran an explicit drawdown-control rule, cutting traded equity by about 20% for every 10% lost, which the paper connects to Grossman and Zhou's 1990s work on optimal drawdown control.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Drawdown de-gearing exists because allocators and pension participants cannot tolerate an 80% drawdown even if the strategy would recover; it is a client constraint, not a maths result.
insights.quote: I think they used a they lost 10% um in the market then they would cut their equity by 20%

insights.claim: The host argues the turtles' genius was never the 100-day breakout entry but the risk approach, and that CTAs are risk managers first because they control the risk taken but not the returns generated.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
insights.so_what: Due diligence on trend managers should weight risk architecture over signal design, since signals are commoditised and risk control is where dispersion comes from.
insights.quote: the genius was not so much in buying a 100 day breakout. The genius was as you point out in the way they approach risk.

themes.theme: AI inside quant research and the junior hiring problem

insights.claim: Moore says the several hundred hours he spent learning Python and pandas at Man Group about seven years ago are now essentially a complete waste given current AI tools.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Implementation skill in quant finance is depreciating fast, which changes both hiring criteria and the cost base of research-heavy managers.
insights.quote: that was essentially a complete waste of time. So to the level that I can program it's absolutely complete useless waste of 200 hours um sort of seven years ago now

insights.claim: The value case for AI in quant research is shifting researchers from roughly 50% creative thinking and 50% implementation to something closer to 90/10, because AI can summarise everything written before but cannot generate brand-new high-alpha quantitative ideas.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: The productivity gain is real but concentrated in commoditised work, so expect research throughput to rise without a proportional rise in genuine alpha discovery.
insights.quote: if you could split that 50/50 and make it more like 9010

insights.claim: Junior and graduate quant roles built around business-as-usual implementation are being squeezed out as processes that used to require humans get automated.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Headcount growth at systematic managers should decouple from AUM growth, and the industry's talent pipeline faces a structural gap at the entry level.
insights.quote: those very junior level graduate type roles where you would spend more time on the kind of BAU implementation etc. like it's kind of being squeezed out by by these tools

insights.claim: Moore's proposed interview method is to hand a candidate an AI-generated piece of work and ask them to critique and improve it, because isolating candidates from AI tools no longer tests real working conditions.
insights.speaker: Harry Moore
insights.so_what: Critical evaluation of machine output is becoming the scarce human skill in research organisations, and firms that test for it will hire better.
insights.quote: locking someone in a Wi-Fi free, computer free box is not a good test of of what working life looks like today
